Are you interesting in evaluating new treatments for pet patients?

Yes. We are interested in oncology candidates with a strong scientific rationale for companion-animal cancer.

### Pet parents

Help us advocate for better cancer treatments. Pet parents play an important role in raising awareness of the need for better and more accessible cancer treatments. By supporting comparative oncology research and sharing trusted information, you can help advance new treatment options for future pet patients.

Help us advocate for better treatment options, raise awareness of comparative oncology and connect pets in need with eligible clinical trials.

#### Taking part in future research

##### Clinical
trial participation

ValiRx Animal Health is not currently recruiting pets into clinical trials. As our programmes progress, future studies may be run through specialist veterinary hospitals and referral centres.

#### Future treatment opportunities

##### Developing tomorrow's veterinary cancer treatments

We are working to adapt promising oncology discoveries for use in companion animals. Our aim is to build the evidence needed to support new veterinary treatments and improve the options available to vets and pet parents.

#### FAQs

Is ValiRx Animal Health currently recruiting pets into clinical trials?

+

No. We will share details through our website, social media and participating veterinary centres when studies become available.

How could my pet be considered for a future trial?

+

Recruitment would take place through participating veterinary hospitals, with eligibility assessed by the treating veterinary team.

Could my pet contribute a sample for research?

+

In some cases, surplus material left after a necessary diagnostic or treatment procedure may be suitable for research.

Can you advise me about my pet's treatment?

+

We cannot provide individual veterinary advice. Please speak to your veterinary surgeon or veterinary oncologist about diagnosis and treatment.

How can I support your work?

+

You can follow our progress on our website and LinkedIn page. Share our work and help raise awareness of comparative oncology.

This study will evaluate whether a single, highly focused dose of radiation can safely treat cancer that has spread to the lungs in dogs. Our radiation treatment is administered externally by delivering high-energy x-rays directly to the tumor so there is no risk of radiation exposure for people in contact with pets receiving this type of therapy. We will assess how practical the treatment is, including treatment planning, managing breathing during radiation for prolonged periods of time, radiation delivery, and the time dogs need to be under anesthesia. The study will also monitor dogs for short- and long-term side effects and evaluate how well the treated tumors respond. Investigators will track how long the treated tumors remain under control and how long the dogs remain free from further cancer progression. The goal is to determine whether this single radiation treatment can safely and effectively control cancerous spread to the lungs.

## Inclusion Criteria

Dogs are eligible for enrollment if they meet all of the following criteria:

  * Confirmed malignancy: Cytologic or histopathologic confirmation of a malignant tumor (e.g., carcinoma, sarcoma, or melanoma) with pulmonary nodules consistent with metastasis to the lungs.

【turn1053search5】 [wordlim: 200] Published: today; Crawled: today; Content type: text/html; 9 hours ago — The goal in managing dogs and cats with cancer is to control pain and improve a patient's overall quality of life by using traditional anticancer therapeutic ... Read more
While pain in certain dogs and cats with cancer will be relieved with treatment directed toward the underlying cancer, others will require symptomatic analgesic therapy to improve their quality of life. A relative abundance of literature discusses the management of cancer pain in people.1-7 In contrast, there is a paucity of information specifically regarding the management of veterinary cancer pain. The most rational way to alleviate cancer pain, whenever possible, is to treat the underlying tumor. Always evaluate the possibility of surgically removing a resectable tumor or obtaining a remission by using radiation therapy for a radiosensitive tumor or chemotherapy for a chemosensitive cancer. While you are waiting for the definitive therapy to take effect and eliminate the source of pain, analgesic and supportive therapies are often required to improve a patient's quality of life. And occasionally, with resistant, refractory, recurring, or terminal cancers, only palliative therapy can truly benefit a patient.

The goal in managing dogs and cats with cancer is to control pain and improve a patient's overall quality of life by using traditional anticancer therapeutic modalities, various analgesic therapies, and supportive care. Before you treat for cancer pain, you must have a basic understanding of the pathophysiology of pain and of the methods used to recognize and evaluate pain in veterinary patients (see the article "Understanding and recognizing cancer pain in dogs and cats").

### TREATMENT DIRECTED AT THE TUMOR

### Surgery

Whenever possible, completely remove a painful tumor surgically. With an appropriate preemptive and multimodal analgesic program in place, including postoperative pain management, most patients with tumors causing pain will be more comfortable after radical surgeries. Surgery is the modality that can most rapidly eliminate the source of pain, and various surgical procedures can be performed, depending on the tumor's type, extent, and location.

# Flow cytometry-based direct antiglobulin test for suspected feline immune-mediated thrombocytopenia: Assay development and demographic factors associated with direct antiglobulin test positivity

Teerawut Nedumpun https://orcid.org/0000-0002-9924-1036 [email protected], Ousakorn Kamenkit, […], Sinittha Thongwandi, Thitima Tripipat, Suwarath Wadeerat, Supanat Boonyapisitsopa, and Napawan Bunpapong+4-4View all authors and affiliations

## Abstract

### Objectives:

This study aimed to develop and evaluate an in-house flow cytometry-based direct antiglobulin test (DAT) for detecting IgG-bound platelets in cats and to investigate the prevalence of DAT positivity and associated risk factors among thrombocytopenic cats.

### Methods:

Platelets were identified by CD41/61 expression, and platelet-bound IgG was assessed using flow cytometry. A diagnostic cutoff for the percentage of IgG-positive platelets was established using 100 healthy cats and preliminarily evaluated in 50 cats with severe thrombocytopenia (platelet count <20,000/µl) before being applied to the remaining 411 thrombocytopenic cats (platelet count <200,000/µl) to determine the prevalence of DAT positivity and its associations with platelet count, breed, age, and sex.

Healthy cats showed 0–10% IgG-positive platelets, and a cutoff of >10% was established. Using this cutoff, 105/461 (22.8%) thrombocytopenic cats were classified as DAT positive. DAT-positive cats had significantly lower platelet counts than DAT-negative cats (median 4000/µl; mean 12,562/µl vs 34,000/µl; mean 47,956/µl; P <0.05), and the percentage of IgG-bound platelets was inversely correlated with platelet count (r = −0.38; P = 0.048). No breed association was identified. Feline immune-mediated thrombocytopenia (IMT; also known as immune thrombocytopenia) is an autoimmune hematologic disorder characterized by increased platelet destruction and, in some cases, reduced platelet production.^{1–3} It may occur as a primary (idiopathic) condition or secondary to underlying causes such as infections, neoplasia, or drugs.^{1} Compared with dogs, primary IMT is uncommon in cats.^{4–6} The pathogenesis of IMT is largely driven by a type II hypersensitivity mechanism, in which a dysregulated humoral immune response promotes the production of autoantibodies directed against platelet antigens.^{7,8} Binding of IgM or IgG autoantibodies to platelets results in opsonization and subsequent clearance by macrophages via Fc receptor-mediated phagocytosis, primarily in the spleen and liver.^{8,9} Complement-mediated mechanisms may further enhance platelet destruction.^{9,10} Cats with IMT typically present with marked thrombocytopenia, with variable and often less overt clinical signs than in dogs.^{4–6} Establishing a definitive diagnosis of IMT in cats remains challenging.^{1,11,12} Routine laboratory testing, including complete blood counts and serum biochemistry, often identifies thrombocytopenia but cannot differentiate immune-mediated platelet destruction from other causes such as consumption, sequestration, decreased production, or pseudothrombocytopenia caused by platelet clumping – a frequent issue in feline samples.^{5,6}

The direct antiglobulin test (DAT), when modified for platelet evaluation, enables detection of immunoglobulins bound in vivo to platelet surfaces and may help confirm a diagnosis of immune-mediated platelet destruction.^{1,4} The presence of IgG bound to platelet membranes has been shown to provide strong evidence supporting feline IMT.^{4,13} Flow cytometry provides a sensitive and quantitative method for identifying IgG-bound platelets using objective fluorescence-based analysis, thereby enhancing diagnostic accuracy compared with conventional techniques.^{3,14–16} The present study aimed to optimize an in-house flow cytometry-based DAT for use in cats, with the goal of establishing a robust and standardized method for identifying immune-mediated platelet destruction and facilitating timely clinical decision-making. To optimize and further assess the flow cytometry-based DAT for detecting platelet-bound IgG in cats with suspected IMT, 461 residual whole blood samples from thrombocytopenic cats were collected from the Veterinary Diagnostic Laboratory (CU VDL). All samples had platelet counts <200,000/µl (Figure 1). Demographic data are presented in Table 1. No live animal handling was involved; therefore, additional ethical approval was not required.

The proportion of feline IgG-positive platelets in 100 healthy cats was in the range of 0–10% (mean 4.5) (Figure 3(a) and (b)). A threshold of >10% IgG-positive platelets was established as the cutoff for subsequent diagnostic interpretation. To preliminarily evaluate the flow cytometry-based DAT for detecting platelet-bound IgG, samples from 50 cats with severe thrombocytopenia (platelet count <20,000/µl) and suspected IMT were analyzed. ImageFigure 3. Determination of cutoff value of the flow cytometry-based direct antiglobulin test (DAT). (a) Representative gating strategy for platelet identification from a healthy cat. (b) Distribution of IgG-bound platelets in healthy cats (n = 100). (c) Representative thrombocytopenic cat (platelet count <20,000/µl) showing increased IgG binding vs isotype control. (d) Distribution of IgG-bound platelets in thrombocytopenic cats (n = 50). Dashed line indicates the 10% cutoff.

The availability of an in-house flow cytometry-based assay may help clinicians to more rapidly identify immune-mediated platelet destruction and support timely decision-making regarding immunosuppressive therapy in appropriate cases. In this study, IgG was selected as the primary target for detection of platelet-bound antibodies.

## Principles of apSTAR

The two principles underlying apSTAR are: local destruction of tumor by means of a laser combined with a photo-absorbing dye and stimulated immune response due to the application of an immunoadjuvant, but also due to increases in antigen accessibility caused by the destruction of the tumor. Both elements of this protocol are crucial. Since this method independently triggers the immune response in each individual, it does not depend upon cross reactivity in the expression of tumor-specific antigen between hosts (as is required in conventional antibody immunotherapy and vaccination.)

## Career and research

LeBlanc was an associate professor with tenure and director of translational research at the University of Tennessee College of Veterinary Medicine (CVM) and University of Tennessee College of Medicine. LeBlanc's group at the University of Tennessee published the first comprehensive studies describing molecular imaging of dogs and cats using PET-CT, focusing on the forward and back-translation of 18F-labelled radiopharmaceuticals.

LeBlanc is a board-certified veterinary oncologist and senior scientist in the molecular imaging program at the National Cancer Institute (NCI). She is director of the NCI's Comparative Oncology Program. Her research focus is in animal modeling for development of new cancer drugs and imaging agents, and identification of imaging biomarkers, development and optimization of PET imaging hardware and imaging protocols. In her position, she oversees and manages the operations of the Comparative Oncology Trials Consortium (COTC), which designs and executes clinical trials of new cancer therapies in tumor-bearing pet dogs.

## Animal testing

The Animals (Scientific Procedures) Act 1986 (ASPA) regulates the conditions under which animal testing can occur in the UK. The UK government that took power in 2024 pledged to stop animal testing for some major safety tests by the end of 2025 and reducing the use of dogs and non-human primates in tests for human medicines by at least 35% by 2030.

Those applying for a licence must explain why such research cannot be done through in vitro (non-animal) methods. All research projects must pass an ethical review panel set by the Home Office, which aims to decide if the potential benefits outweigh any suffering for the animals involved.

Primates, cats, dogs, and horses have additional protection over other vertebrates included in the Act. Revised legislation came into force in January 2013. This has been expanded to protect "all living vertebrates, other than man, and any living cephalopod.

GraphBEAT: Graph-based Bucketized Event Aggregation Over Time for Early Risk Stratification of Gastrointestinal Cancers (https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.22014)
【turn1053academia24】 [wordlim: 200] Published: 6 days ago; 
Title: GraphBEAT: Graph-based Bucketized Event Aggregation Over Time for Early Risk Stratification of Gastrointestinal Cancers
Authors: Leo Y. Li-Han, Chris Varghese, Elizabeth B. Habermann, Mark J. Truty, William R. G. Perry, Cornelius A. Thiels, Hojjat Salehinejad
Date: Thu Oct 15 14:55:39 2026

Longitudinal electronic health records (EHRs) contain complementary diagnostic and laboratory information about patient health. However, irregularity, sparsity, heterogeneity, and incompleteness in documentation complicate EHR modeling. To address the problem, we introduce GraphBEAT (Graph-based Bucketized Event Aggregation over Time), a temporal graph representation learning framework that groups clinical events into time buckets and transforms observed features into patient-specific, temporally directed graphs to enable early risk stratification for gastrointestinal cancers. Each node in an EHR graph encodes feature identity, observed value, and temporal position of clinical events. A context-aware, time-decay message-passing mechanism models transitions between successive buckets, followed by multi-head attention pooling to generate patient-level representations. GraphBEAT was trained and evaluated on multi-site longitudinal diagnosis codes and laboratory tests to predict pancreatic, liver, and intestinal cancer at 12-, 24-, and 36-month diagnostic lead times. In all experimental setups, GraphBEAT consistently outperformed baseline graph neural networks (GraphSAGE, GAT, and GCN) and sequence modeling approaches (Transformer and long short-term memory [LSTM]). GraphBEAT also required over 250x fewer floating-point operations per patient and over 20x fewer parameters than the Transformer and LSTM baselines. These results support GraphBEAT as an accurate and computationally efficient approach for cancer risk stratification from sparse, heterogeneous longitudinal health records.

Title: Pathology foundation models for training-free case retrieval in salivary gland tumors
Authors: Maximilian J. Roesel, Niklas Kiermeyer, Philipp Keyl, Frederick Klauschen
Date: Thu Oct 15 15:40:48 2026

In pathology, pattern recognition relies on a frame of reference built through extensive training and experience, which may still fall short when encountering rare cancer subtypes. Archives of previously diagnosed tumors often contain relevant precedents, yet identifying the most relevant cases remains challenging. Here we explore whether content-based retrieval with current pathology foundation models facilitates rare cancer diagnostics without any task-specific training. Pathologists can query a digitized archive using a region of interest (ROI) from a whole slide image (WSI) and retrieve morphologically similar cases, along with their ICD-O codes and corresponding WSIs. The ROI can be selected manually or automatically using a gated attention-based multiple instance learning model. We evaluate our approach by leave-one-case-out on an imbalanced dataset of 137 salivary gland tumor cases spanning 12 ICD-O morphology categories, comparing four pathology foundation models (Atlas2, Atlas2-B, Atlas2-S, and UNI2h). Top-1/3/5 retrieval was 62.5%/76.7%/81.3% for Atlas2, 50.2/66.6/72.9% for UNI2h, 52.3%/71.5%/77.6% for Atlas2-B and 54.4/65.2/73.7% for Atlas2-S. Macro-averaged F1 ranged from 69.0% for the smallest model Atlas2-S to 76.6% for the largest model Atlas2 across the five classes with at least ten cases. Our modified Chamfer similarity separated correct from incorrect matches among the Top-5 more reliably for Atlas2 (AUC 0.754) than for Atlas2-B (0.679, p = 0.020) and Atlas2-S (0.653, p = 0.003), but not UNI2h (0.697, p = 0.196). Requiring no additional training or manual annotation, this approach makes departmental archives searchable with pathology foundation models, providing a low-barrier route to case-based differential diagnosis and extending the individual frame of reference to the collective experience of the department.

FDE-Gym: The Last Mile of AI Delivery (https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.22350)
【turn1053academia26】 [wordlim: 200] Published: 6 days ago; 
Title: FDE-Gym: The Last Mile of AI Delivery
Authors: Dongxu Yang, Hongda Yan, Renxin Wang, Baoli Zhang, Haojia Zuo, Ying Zhao, Youmin Chen, Xiaojian Liao, Congming Gao, Tianyang Jiang, Yixiao Chen, Qing Wang, Zhiguo Yu, Xiaqing Li, Yuhao Zhang, Jiawen Sun, Renzhe Xu, De Mi, Tiancheng Wu, Xianya Fu, Xuanlu Zhao, Bo Feng, Meixuan Ren, Guanming Lin, Ziheng Zhou, Xinhua Wang
Date: Thu Oct 15 17:57:23 2026

Existing agent benchmarks typically evaluate agents on well-specified tasks defined by issue reports, specifications, or task tickets. Real-world customer delivery is different: forward-deployed engineers (FDEs) must clarify ambiguous requirements, work in live systems, and uncover unstated constraints. We introduce FDE-Gym, a benchmark of 95 end-to-end delivery tasks from 20 customer scenarios across 18 sectors, each adapted by industry experts from real-world delivery projects. In simulated customer environments with scripted stakeholders and modifiable customer systems, agents interact with stakeholders and operate on production-like systems to deliver working solutions. FDE-Gym scores a delivery by how much it improves the customer's own success metric, normalized between 0 (unchanged system) and 1 (reference solution), with penalties for stakeholder interactions (messages, trial runs, and waiting time). An online platform lets humans practice FDE skills under the same grading criteria. We evaluate 13 model configurations from seven providers. In the realistic setting, where unstated constraints must be discovered, the best configuration achieves a mean FDE-Gym score of 0.56 and resolves only 14 of the 95 tasks (a score of at least 0.8 with no incident). Discovering unstated constraints is the primary bottleneck: performance drops sharply when models must uncover them without explicit guidance. Yet information discovery alone does not account for the gap: even on the 23 tasks where the best configuration obtains every key fact from stakeholders, it reaches a normalized business uplift of 0.8 or above on only 10. These results reveal a substantial gap between solving well-specified tasks and delivering effective AI systems for real customers.

Objective: Trofinetide, approved in 2023 as the first Rett syndrome treatment, lacks scalable real-world monitoring because chart review is labor-intensive. We developed a dual large language model (LLM) consensus pipeline to extract 18 treatment-response phenotypes, comprising 4 adverse effects, 13 Rett clinical features, and medication refusal, from clinical notes. Materials and Methods: We analyzed 26,763 notes from 108 patients with confirmed sustained trofinetide exposure at Texas Children's Hospital. The pipeline filters notes by keyword, classifies each through two LLMs requiring consensus, and aggregates a patient-by-timepoint matrix. Architecture and prompt were selected on a diarrhea development set, then frozen and applied to the other 17 phenotypes with the phenotype definition substituted, as an out-of-sample test. The reported prompt comparison scores 183 expert-labeled cells. Results: A prompt requiring diarrhea to be active and severe performed best (84.2 $\pm$ 0.0% accuracy; F1 = 0.674), 47 percentage points above regular-expression matching ($p < 0.0001$). Expert reviewers judged six of the pipeline's calls per phenotype, three positive and three negative, and agreed with 90.2% (92/102). The 13 Rett clinical features are manifestations of the disorder itself rather than adverse effects of trofinetide. Gross and fine motor impairment, language/communication, and stereotypy were documented present in 92-100% of patients at every visit. Discussion: In-context LLM extraction captured multi-domain treatment responses. The outcome is documented presence at each visit, not a direction-of-change judgment. Conclusion: Coupling in-context LLM reasoning with a consensus architecture offers a scalable alternative to keyword and regular-expression extraction for real-world evidence, adapting to new phenotypes and medications through configuration alone.
